title: Household liquidity coverage depends on whether disposable income and short-term credit are counted
geography: United States; households in the JPMorganChase Institute administrative-data analysis
method: JPMorganChase Institute administrative-data analysis of household cash savings, disposable income, and short-term credit capacity.
method_change_notes: The official landing page adds Figure 6, a monthly line chart for January 2022 through December 2023 by income quartile, plus a text transcript describing steady levels and seasonal dips around tax-refund months. The chart is published as a raster image without a downloadable numeric table, so exact monthly values are not transcribed into this record.
uncertainty: The snapshot does not provide a reproducible public variance extract or a common denominator definition that can be pooled with SHED adult estimates or USDA household food-security estimates.
counterinterpretation: Broader liquidity access produces a materially higher coverage estimate than cash savings alone; financial room depends on the resource definition and cannot be inferred from a single cash-only measure.

related_sources.claim: Official research snapshot with December 2023 household liquidity estimates.
Official research landing page with Figure 6 monthly chart and text transcript.

chart_asset.measure: share of households unable to cover an unexpected $400 expense, by income quartile
chart_asset.qualitative_transcript: Low-income inability hovers around 25 percent with seasonal dips around April; each income group remains broadly steady during 2022 and 2023.

boundary: This is an independent mechanism challenge, not a pooled U.S. trend estimate, causal result, qualified trend, or company exposure finding. The source snapshot carries a written republication restriction.
